title: A NATO ally holds the key to Europe’s drone wall, and it isn’t Washington
gist: NATO's Ankara summit pledged more than forty billion dollars over five years for counterdrone defense while the EU promises a fully functional drone wall by end-2027 — on an industrial base that builds no combat-proven armed drone at scale and whose flagship Eurodrone has slipped and lost France. Tolga Demiryol argues the only allied industry that can deliver at cost and speed is Turkey's (arms exports up 122 percent, Baykar at roughly $1.9 billion of 2024 revenue), and that Europe's real choice is whether Turkish capacity enters under negotiated rules or, as now, through a back door with none.

insights.claim: At the July 7-8 NATO summit in Ankara, allies made counterdrone defense the signature industrial commitment, pledging more than forty billion dollars over five years, a new NATO counterdrone marketplace, and a fivefold increase in drone-operator training by the end of 2027.
insights.speaker: Tolga Demiryol
insights.so_what: A sized, dated procurement pool — the addressable market for counterdrone detection, jamming and interceptor suppliers over five years.
insights.locator: When NATO leaders gathered in Ankara on July 7–8

insights.claim: The International Institute for Strategic Studies has counted 144 drone incidents across thirteen European states in eighteen months since Russian drones crossed into Poland in September 2025, with sightings closing airports from Copenhagen to Munich and imposing cancellation and diversion costs out of all proportion to intruders that often carried no warhead.
insights.speaker: Tolga Demiryol
insights.so_what: Quantifies the cost-asymmetry problem driving spend: cheap intrusions generate disproportionate civil-aviation losses, guaranteeing sustained counterdrone budgets.
insights.locator: Since Russian drones crossed into Poland in September 2025

insights.claim: Europe builds no combat-proven armed drone at scale, fields no drone exporter of global consequence, and runs a counterdrone sector fragmented across numerous national programs, while its flagship Eurodrone has slipped by years and just lost France's participation.
insights.speaker: Tolga Demiryol
insights.so_what: The capability gap is structural, not budgetary — meaning European funds will flow to non-European or joint-venture suppliers regardless of local-content preferences.
insights.quote: Money is arriving, but money is not yet capacity, and the wall’s deadline is eighteen months away.
insights.locator: There is a pressing question of capacity

insights.claim: Helsing's CA-1 Europa, one of the most ambitious European combat-drone projects, is not due to fly until 2027 and its electronic-attack variant is not due in service until 2031 — four years after the EU's drone wall is meant to be finished.
insights.speaker: Tolga Demiryol
insights.so_what: The timeline mismatch between Europe's most-hyped defense-tech program and its own deadline is the clearest evidence the wall will be built with imported capacity.
insights.locator: Even Helsing’s CA-1 Europa

insights.claim: US and Israeli counterdrone systems are priced backwards for the threat — a Patriot missile runs to roughly four million dollars and even Raytheon's purpose-built Coyote interceptor costs about $100,000 — which is why the Pentagon itself has moved to buy Ukrainian interceptors costing about a thousand dollars apiece.
insights.speaker: Tolga Demiryol
insights.so_what: A three-order-of-magnitude cost spread that will restructure the counterdrone vendor landscape away from legacy missile primes toward volume-priced effectors.
insights.quote: the interceptor costs far more than the drone it stops
insights.locator: Europe has three ways to erect a drone wall

insights.claim: Ukraine now builds interceptor drones costing between 1,000 and 4,000 euros ($1,142 and $4,567) against Shahed-class weapons costing tens of thousands of euros, and produced roughly 100,000 of them in 2025.
insights.speaker: Tolga Demiryol
insights.so_what: Ukraine has demonstrated favorable cost exchange at scale — the benchmark any European counterdrone program must match to be credible.
insights.locator: Dollars and sense

insights.claim: Buying Ukrainian has serious limitations because Ukraine's production is claimed first by its own war and its factories operate within Russian strike range.
insights.speaker: Tolga Demiryol
insights.so_what: Rules out Ukraine as Europe's primary counterdrone supplier and explains why a third production anchor is needed.
insights.locator: Buying Ukrainian, however, has serious limitations

insights.claim: The systems that win the drone fight are cheap, iterated at speed and built at volume — precisely the profile of the Turkish and Ukrainian industries and precisely not that of Europe's deliberate, slow-moving procurement.
insights.speaker: Tolga Demiryol
insights.so_what: A screening criterion for counterdrone suppliers: unit cost and iteration cadence, not platform sophistication.
insights.locator: The systems that win this fight are cheap

insights.claim: Turkey's arms exports grew 122 percent between 2016-20 and 2021-25, and it is now one of a handful of states dominating the global combat drone market, with its uncrewed combat aircraft reaching more than thirty countries including six NATO allies — Poland first, then Romania.
insights.speaker: Tolga Demiryol
insights.so_what: Establishes Turkey as an existing NATO-interoperable supplier with installed base, lowering the integration barrier relative to new European entrants.
insights.locator: The track record of Turkey’s defense industry is impressive

insights.claim: Baykar reportedly earned roughly $1.9 billion in 2024, almost all of it from exports, producing combat-proven, NATO-interoperable systems priced at a fraction of Western equivalents.
insights.speaker: Tolga Demiryol
insights.so_what: Sizes the private Turkish champion that would capture European drone-wall spend, and its export-only revenue base makes it dependent on exactly this market access.
insights.locator: Baykar reportedly earned roughly $1.9 billion in 2024

insights.claim: The counterdrone portfolio the EU's drone wall most needs comes from Turkey's Aselsan — layered detection, jamming and laser systems that matured alongside Baykar's drones.
insights.speaker: Tolga Demiryol
insights.so_what: Names the specific counterdrone supplier positioned to win EU drone wall workshare — Aselsan, not just Baykar.
insights.locator: The counterdrone portfolio the EU’s drone wall most needs

insights.claim: Turkey's drawback is political rather than financial: it stands outside the EU's defense-industrial architecture and is excluded from the SAFE procurement instrument, so bringing its capacity in requires terms the EU has yet to set.
insights.speaker: Tolga Demiryol
insights.so_what: SAFE eligibility is the single regulatory switch that would reprice Turkish defense exposure — a concrete policy catalyst to watch.
insights.locator: In terms of capability, cost, and speed

themes.theme: Turkish capacity already entering via the back door

insights.claim: Baykar has acquired Italy's Piaggio Aerospace, which means its Bayraktar TB2 and Akinci can conceivably be built on EU territory.
insights.speaker: Tolga Demiryol
insights.so_what: A completed corporate transaction that converts Turkish drones into EU-origin production — the mechanism by which local-content rules get bypassed.
insights.locator: Yet interfirm cooperation is already underway

insights.claim: In June 2026 Rome cleared a joint venture between Baykar and Leonardo with sales restricted to NATO customers, a month after the two flew their first crewed-uncrewed teaming trial in which a Leonardo trainer commanded a Baykar Kizilelma jet drone.
insights.speaker: Tolga Demiryol
insights.so_what: A live, cleared JV with a European prime — the template other member states are likely to copy, and a channel for Leonardo to gain drone capability.
insights.locator: In June 2026, Rome cleared a joint venture

insights.claim: The EU's local-content rules and vetoes on Turkish association have not kept Turkish capacity out of Europe; they have kept it ungoverned, integrated case by case through national investment screens and corporate deals with no common terms.
insights.speaker: Tolga Demiryol
insights.so_what: Exclusion policy is failing on its own terms, so the base case is deeper Turkish penetration of European defense supply chains regardless of Brussels' stance.
insights.quote: they have kept it ungoverned, integrated case by case through national investment screens and corporate deals, with no common terms
insights.locator: The EU’s local-content rules and its vetoes

insights.claim: By integrating rather than importing Turkish capacity — via joint ventures with European firms using European engines and optics — the relationship becomes one of interdependence rather than one-way dependence, unlike buying from the US or Israel.
insights.speaker: Tolga Demiryol
insights.so_what: Explains why European engine and optics suppliers are second-order beneficiaries of any Turkish integration deal.
insights.locator: The Turkish option is not free of autonomy costs either

themes.theme: The two-track problem and proposed terms

insights.claim: Europe is building the same counterdrone capability along two tracks with different memberships — a NATO undertaking including Turkey and a Strategy for Industry-NATO Cooperation plus an Innovation Scale-Up Package whose NATO Engine will pool spare production capacity across the alliance including Ukraine, running alongside an EU drone wall from which Turkey is excluded.
insights.speaker: Tolga Demiryol
insights.so_what: Duplicated institutional tracks mean vendors face two different qualification paths; the NATO route is the faster one for non-EU suppliers.
insights.locator: The counterdrone commitments unveiled at the summit

insights.claim: The Turkey exclusion asymmetry is a European problem more than a transatlantic one, because on the NATO track Washington and Ankara already sit on the same side in the same marketplace drawing on the same production network — it is only inside European instruments that Turkey has no settled place.
insights.speaker: Tolga Demiryol
insights.so_what: Reframes Turkey's exclusion as self-inflicted European cost rather than allied consensus — raising odds of eventual EU accommodation.
insights.locator: That asymmetry is a European problem more than a transatlantic one

insights.claim: Drones and counterdrone systems should be treated as the pilot sector for third-country access to the EU defense-industrial architecture, negotiating Turkish access terms for this one sector where need is most urgent and the advantage clearest before generalizing.
insights.speaker: Tolga Demiryol
insights.so_what: A sector-first path that could produce a concrete Turkish market-access decision far sooner than a wholesale association settlement.
insights.locator: What to do now

insights.claim: The counterdrone layer should be built as a triangle of complementary strengths: the EU as market and financier, Ukraine as the combat laboratory where interceptor designs are tested and repriced against live threats, and Turkey as production anchor.
insights.speaker: Tolga Demiryol
insights.so_what: A clean map of who captures which role and margin in European counterdrone — useful for allocating exposure across the three geographies.
insights.locator: Building the counterdrone layer as a triangle

insights.claim: The bargain should be stated as reciprocity between equals: Turkey accepts program-level end-use and reporting commitments, receiving predictability and settled standing in the European market on the same association terms the EU already extended to Canada.
insights.speaker: Tolga Demiryol
insights.so_what: The Canada precedent gives a concrete legal template, making a Turkish association deal more tractable than it appears.
insights.locator: Stating the bargain plainly, as reciprocity between equals

insights.claim: Europe has committed to fielding a continental counterdrone defense by the end of 2027 on an industrial base that has never built one, so the wall — if built on time — will be built with capacity Europe does not yet possess, and the only question in Europe's control is whether that capacity arrives under rules written in advance or through a back door with no rules at all.
insights.speaker: Tolga Demiryol
insights.so_what: The central forecast: foreign capacity fills the gap either way, so bet on Turkish and Ukrainian suppliers gaining European share rather than on EU primes scaling in time.
insights.quote: The only question within Europe’s control is whether that capacity arrives under rules written in advance or, as now, through a back door with no rules at all.
insights.locator: The wall will be built, if it is built on time
